name: Cat-eye frames for men

card.summary: Cat-eye frames have an upward sweep at the outer corners that draws the eye line up and out, which wearers use to add lift and angularity to the upper face.

quick.overview:
Cat-eye frames are glasses whose outer edges sweep upward where the front meets the temples. The shape emphasises the brow and outer eye corner, which people in style communities use to give the eyes a lifted, more angular look.

The style came from women's eyewear of the 1930s to 1960s and returned in the 1990s and late 2010s. Men's versions are usually more restrained, with thinner or squarer upswept lines. No studies have examined how the frame shape changes perceived attractiveness.
quick.how: Wearers pick a pair with a subtle upswept outer edge, often in acetate or metal, and match it to face shape. Some choose frames that echo a strong brow line or counter a rounder face with a more angular silhouette.
quick.risks: There is no health risk beyond ordinary eyewear considerations such as correct prescription and fit. Style outcomes depend on face shape and personal taste, and a strongly upswept frame may read as a fashion statement.

lead: Cat-eye frames are eyeglasses and sunglasses whose defining feature is an upward sweep at the outer edges, where the temples meet the front. They are closely related to browline glasses.[1]

People use them to visually lift the outer eye, draw attention to the brow and add angular contrast to a softer face. The style is historically feminine: American Optical released the Ful-Vue in 1931, and stars such as Audrey Hepburn and Marilyn Monroe popularised the shape in the 1950s and 1960s, before it returned in the 1990s and again in the late 2010s.[1]
Men's looksmaxxing and style discussions adapt the shape in more subtle forms. No published trial has tested how frame shape affects the perceived attractiveness of men.

angle.text: Wearers choose cat-eye or subtly upswept frames to add the impression of lift at the outer eye and a sharper brow line. The effect comes from the frame geometry and is present only while the glasses are worn.

paras: The upward sweep at the outer edges is the signature of the cat-eye shape, and the style predates the oversized bug-eye frames of the 1970s through 1990s.[1]

In 1931 American Optical released the Ful-Vue with hinges set high on the frame, an early precursor. Window dresser Altina Schinasi later designed the Harlequin frame, and American Optical released a version with Claire McCardell in 1952.[1]
The style fell out of fashion after the 1960s, returned in the 1990s, and re-emerged in the late 2010s; by 2024 Meta and Ray-Ban had introduced a cat-eye smartglasses frame.[1]
Wikipedia notes at least one male wearer, the chemist Otto Wichterle.[1] In current men's style, narrower or squarer versions with a mild upward flick are used to sharpen the upper face.

timeline.event: American Optical releases the Ful-Vue frame with high hinges.[1]
